products.name: Obsidian AI
products.note: Local-first knowledge AI; plugins; privacy-focused; no cloud dependency

reading.body:
Obsidian's AI strategy centers on local-first processing: all computation happens on the user's device with no data sent to Obsidian's servers, reversing the cloud-dependent model that dominates AI products.

This approach trades cloud infrastructure costs for client-side compute. The user's machine becomes the binding resource instead of server capacity and bandwidth. The two registered MCP servers suggest the company is enabling AI assistants to access Obsidian vaults through standard protocols, but the fundamental claim remains that processing stays local. For builders of AI systems, this means Obsidian users cannot be counted as load on data center power budgets the way cloud-hosted AI products can be.

The data does not specify what compute requirements Obsidian AI actually demands on user devices, whether the model runs locally or calls remote APIs despite the privacy claim, or how the company monetizes a freemium product without the operational advantages of centralized compute. The local-first model works only if users have sufficient hardware, a constraint that differs from grid-dependent infrastructure but remains a constraint nonetheless.

profile_text.body:
Obsidian is a for-profit startup founded in 2020 and headquartered in Los Angeles, California. The company makes a note-taking and knowledge management application that, as its site describes, stores notes privately on the user's device so they can be accessed quickly and offline, with no server-side access to the content. The application is positioned as a flexible tool for personal notes, journaling, knowledge bases, and project management, and it allows users to create linked connections between notes, visualize those relationships through an interactive graph, and extend functionality through thousands of community plugins and an open API.

The site's tracked AI product, listed as Obsidian AI, is described as a local-first knowledge AI that is privacy-focused and carries no cloud dependency, consistent with the company's broader emphasis on keeping data on the user's device. Two third-party MCP servers associated with the platform appear in the registry: one designed to connect AI assistants to a GitHub-hosted Obsidian vault for access and search, and another for searching a vault by title or keyword and summarizing related content. No litigation or SEC filings are recorded in the held facts, though the company carries a California legal exposure count of 181.
